elements.id-string-19: Handling moving and movable objects is an important problem that has major applications in navigation and allied tasks.
elements.id-string-20: Most existing techniques focus on extracting and removing moving objects while using only static structures for navigation \cite{ruchti2018mapping,chen2021moving,nishio2022moving,pfreundschuh2021dynamic,tian2022dl}.
elements.id-string-21: They do so by using labeled segmentation and object information to train a model to identify moving objects.
elements.id-string-22: However, everyday navigation scenarios come across \textit{potentially movable} objects.
elements.id-string-23: Such objects have the capacity to move but may appear stationary at a given instant and hence are a potential hazard to downstream navigation-based tasks.
elements.id-string-24: When moving, these objects also add to the moving parts of a scene, thereby adding to the Absolute Translation Error \cite{sturm2012benchmark} and Relative Pose Error \cite{sturm2012benchmark} during pose estimation  \cite{kumar2021dslr}.

elements.id-string-29: Central to our task of discriminating \textit{dynamic objects (moving and movable)} from \textit{static (non-movable)} objects is the design of the discriminator.
elements.id-string-30: For this task, we require the availability of LiDAR scans that are only composed of only static structures in a given environment, which we refer to as \textit{static scans}.

elements.id-string-39: In this work, we address the aforementioned issues and propose the following contributions:
elements.id-string-41: We present \dslr{}, a GAN-based adversarial model for \textit{generating static background} of occluded parts of a dynamic LiDAR scan and henceforth \textit{segmenting out moving and movable  parts of scenes}.
elements.id-string-42: This is achieved in a segmentation label-free manner.
elements.id-string-43: \dslr{} uses a novel couple discriminator to discriminate carefully chosen pairs of static and dynamic scans.
elements.id-string-44: The novel design choice of the input helps our model to explicitly focus its attention on moving as well as movable objects, without any external supervision.To reinforce the attention of our couple discriminator on moving and movable objects, we design a novel contrastive strategy.

elements.id-string-308: Accurate static structure reconstruction and segmentation of non-stationary objects is of vital importance for autonomous navigation applications.
elements.id-string-309: These applications \textit{assume} a LiDAR scan to consist of only static structures.
elements.id-string-310: In the real world however, LiDAR scans consist of non-stationary dynamic structures - moving and \textit{movable} objects.
elements.id-string-311: Current solutions use segmentation information to isolate and remove moving structures from LiDAR scan.
elements.id-string-312: This strategy fails in several important use-cases where segmentation information is not available.
elements.id-string-313: In such scenarios, moving objects and objects with high uncertainty in their motion \textit{i.e. movable objects}, may escape detection.
elements.id-string-315: We present \dslr{}, a novel GAN based adversarial model that segments out moving as well as movable objects in the absence of segmentation information.
elements.id-string-316: We achieve this by accurately transforming a dynamic LiDAR scan to its corresponding static scan.
elements.id-string-317: This is obtained by replacing dynamic objects and corresponding occlusions with static structures which were occluded by dynamic objects.
elements.id-string-318: We leverage corresponding static-dynamic LiDAR pairs.
elements.id-string-319: We design a novel discriminator, coupled with a contrastive loss on a smartly selected LiDAR scan triplet.
elements.id-string-320: For datasets lacking paired information, we propose \dslruda{} that integrates Unsupervised Domain Adaptation into the network.
elements.id-string-321: We perform rigorous experiments to demonstrate state of the art dynamic to static translation performance on a sparse real world industrial dataset, an urban and a simulated dataset.
elements.id-string-322: \dslr{} also segments out movable and moving objects without using segmentation information.
elements.id-string-323: Without utilizing segmentation labels, \dslr{} performs better than segmentation based navigation baseline in \textit{highly dynamic} and \textit{long} LiDAR sequences.

elements.id-string-327: Handling non-stationary objects is an important problem with major applications for LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) based Autonomous Vehicles (AVs).
elements.id-string-328: Current solutions extract existing static structures by segmenting and removing moving objects  (\citet{chen2021moving}) with the help of segmentation and object information.
elements.id-string-329: They use this information to train a model to identify and remove moving objects in real time.
elements.id-string-330: Collecting segmentation labels is laborious, expensive and time-consuming, especially for several popular and important settings like industrial environments, fulfilment centers, urban settings, etc.
elements.id-string-331: In addition, common everyday scenarios also involve \textit{movable} objects.
elements.id-string-332: They have the capacity to move but may be stationary at a given instant, and can escape detection in segmentation label free settings due to uncertain motion.
elements.id-string-333: When moving, these objects add to the moving parts of a scene, thereby leading to erroneous pose estimates.
elements.id-string-334: Thus, they are a potential hazard to AVs.
elements.id-string-335: We address the above issues by proposing \dslr{}, a GAN based generative network that enables precise segmentation of dynamic - movable as well as moving objects.
elements.id-string-336: This is achieved in the absence of any form of segmentation information, by generating corresponding static reconstructions for a given dynamic LiDAR scan (Figure \ref{fig:movable-first}).
elements.id-string-337: \dslr{} is trained with corresponding static and dynamic LiDAR scan pairs which are easier to collect and are time and cost effective (\citet{dslr-git}) as compared to labelled information collection.
elements.id-string-338: In \dslr{}, we introduce an intuitively designed discriminator that enforces an implicit attention to dynamic objects.
elements.id-string-339: This is coupled with an intuitively designed contrastive strategy that reinforces the dissimilarity between dynamic and static scans.
elements.id-string-340: We list the contributions of our work here:
elements.id-string-341: We present \dslr{}, a GAN-based adversarial model for \textit{generating static background} of occluded parts of a dynamic LiDAR scan (dynamic to static translation) and henceforth \textit{segmenting out moving and movable  parts of scenes}.
elements.id-string-342: This is achieved in a segmentation-label devoid setting.
elements.id-string-343: \dslr{} uses a novel couple discriminator to discriminate carefully chosen pairs of static and dynamic input.
elements.id-string-344: This design choice helps our model to explicitly focus its attention on moving as well as movable objects, without external supervision.To reinforce the attention of our couple discriminator on the pattern of moving and movable objects, we design a novel contrastive strategy.
elements.id-string-345: We utilize static-dynamic LiDAR correspondence to design hard negative triplets of scans for contrastive learning.We quantitatively demonstrate the superior quality of static reconstructions on 3 varied datasets.
elements.id-string-346: We qualitatively demonstrate the usefulness of \dslr{} in segmenting out movable as well as moving objects without using segmentation labels.To work well with datasets lacking static-dynamic correspondence, we propose \dslruda{}.
elements.id-string-347: We use Unsupervised Domain Adaptation to adapt models trained on correspondence datasets to datasets lacking correspondence.
elements.id-string-348: Despite working in segmentation devoid settings, \dslruda{} performs comparable to or better than segmentation based baselines for navigation in long sequences with \textit{highly dynamic environments}.
elements.id-string-349: Generative modeling for LiDAR has seen considerable development with the advent of several pattern recognition systems - diffusion models, generative models, etc.
elements.id-string-350: They use LiDAR point cloud or range image representation for underlying pattern recognition and modelling of LiDAR.
elements.id-string-351: Generating occluded static parts of scenes has been explored for several modalities: images, point clouds and recently LiDAR.
elements.id-string-353: (\citet{wang2022coarse}) propose a coarse-to-fine network for dynamic-to-static image translation, without any segmentation information and show impressive results.
elements.id-string-354: (\citet{ahn2023unsupervised}) propose to inpaint a dynamic semantic segmentation mask by replacing dynamic objects based labels with static object labels.
elements.id-string-355: For point clouds, (\citet{fei2023dctr}) address the problem of unstructuerd point prediction in lcoal patches and the inefficient utilization of local features.
elements.id-string-356: They propose a dual channel transformer that leverages point and channel-wise attention to generate locally compact and structured point clouds.
elements.id-string-357: (\citet{li2023progressive}) model the point cloud generation process a two-level hierarchy of distributions to learn the pattern of the point clouds.
elements.id-string-358: They propose a hierarchical consistency variational autoencoder that ensures that  the fine-grained parts and underlying shape and can be reconstructed with high precision.
elements.id-string-359: \citet{zhang2023learning} alleviate distortion of geometric details by formulating the  point cloud completion as a geometric transformation problem.
elements.id-string-360: They exploit repetitive geometric structures in 3D shapes to generate complete shapes.
elements.id-string-361: (\citet{zhang2021unsupervised}) uses GAN inversion for point cloud completion and shows remarkable results on standard shape datasets.

elements.id-string-375: Most static translation methods for point clouds discussed above focus on enhancing the power of the generator.
elements.id-string-376: Our focus is to enable the discriminator to learn precise discriminatory features between static and dynamic LIDAR scans - moving and movable objects.
elements.id-string-377: Contrastive Learning focus on learning rich patterns in data by grouping samples with the same labels together while distancing out dissimilar ones.
elements.id-string-378: Some well-known contrastive losses include Maximum Margin Contrastive Loss (\citet{hadsell2006dimensionality}), Triplet Loss (\citet{weinberger2009distance}) and multi-class N-pair loss (\citet{sohn2016improved}).
elements.id-string-379: Triplet Loss operates on a triplet of latent vectors.
elements.id-string-380: The objective of triplet loss is to find patterns in the dataset that keep the positive sample within an $\alpha$-neighborhood of the anchor while forcing the negative sample out of the $\alpha$-neighborhood, $\alpha$ being a margin hyperparamter.
elements.id-string-381: Contrastive Learning with hard negatives (\citet{robinson2020contrastive}) involves selecting negative samples that are difficult to distinguish from the anchor sample.
elements.id-string-382: Several approaches (\citet{xie2022delving}) deploy hard negative mining for contrastive learning in order to learn better representations for downstream tasks.
elements.id-string-384: Throughout our paper, a corresponding static-dynamic LiDAR scan pair, refers to a LiDAR scan pair $(s_i, d_i)$ where both the scans share exactly the same surrounding.
elements.id-string-385: The only difference is that $d_i$ consists of movable and moving objects, unlike $s_i$ (Figure \ref{fig:movable-first}).
elements.id-string-386: We have a set of static scans $\textbf{St}=(s_i, i: 0,1,2...)$ and corresponding dynamic scans denoted as $\textbf{Dy}=(d_i, i: 0,1,2...)$.
elements.id-string-387: Given a dynamic scan $d_i$, and its latent representation on the dynamic manifold, ($r_{d_i}$): our goal is to map $r_{d_i}$  to its closest corresponding point ($\overline{r}_{s_i}$) on the static manifold.
elements.id-string-388: $\overline{r}_{s_i}$ must produce the closest corresponding static LiDAR $\overline{s}_{i}$, by generating static background of the occluded regions, as seen in $s_i$.
elements.id-string-389: We achieve this by developing a novel discriminator and a contrastive strategy that allows precise discrimination of dynamic objects and occlusions from static objects and occlusions.
elements.id-string-390: The generated static structures along with the input dynamic LiDAR are used for movable and moving object segmentation.
elements.id-string-392: We describe \dslr{}'s architecture here - generator, discriminator, contrastive learning for the discriminator and the training setup for MOVES, below.
elements.id-string-394: We use range image-based LiDAR preprocessing, which allows us to use image-based processing on LiDAR effectively.
elements.id-string-395: We use a conditional GAN architecture for the  static translation.
elements.id-string-396: We use the Encoder ($E_\phi$) and Decoder ($D_\theta$) from (\citet{caccia2018deep}) for our generator (\textit{G}).

elements.id-string-399: We provide an overview of the challenges while designing the discriminator.
elements.id-string-400: \textbf{(1)} Discriminating a static scan ($s_i$) from the dynamic scan ($d_i$) is challenging because both are generated from similar LiDAR distribution and share similar patterns - scenes and structure.
elements.id-string-401: Dynamic LiDAR scans are equivalent to static LiDAR with noise in the form of dynamic objects.
elements.id-string-402: Latent feature vectors of both consists of mostly homogeneous and almost indistinguishable patterns.
elements.id-string-403: Features and patterns that help in discrimination (i.e. dynamic objects and occlusions) are limited because they occupy a small percentage of points in the scan compared to the common static regions.
elements.id-string-404: This leads to an imbalance w.r.t.
elements.id-string-405: the discriminatory features, making them difficult to learn.
elements.id-string-406: \textbf{(2)} A vanilla discriminator for static scans \textit{v/s} dynamic scans, suffers from a \textit{simplicity bias} (\citet{shah2020pitfalls}) - the discriminator needs to only pay attention to the \textit{simplest features} for discrimination i.e. (moving objects), to distinguish them from static scans.
elements.id-string-407: It saturates prematurely by learning these simplest features.
elements.id-string-408: Movable objects (which are difficult to discover due to uncertain motion) do not contribute significantly to the learning because the model never needs to use these complex movable object features.
elements.id-string-409: This leads to  sub-optimal translations as shown in Ablation studies (using a GAN with a vanilla discriminator) (Section \ref{sec:ablation} and Table \ref{tab:ablation-disc}).
elements.id-string-410: To address the above challenges, we design a novel \textit{couple discriminator} ($D$) for our proposed GAN, which operates on the latent space of the LiDAR scans.
elements.id-string-411: $D$ takes a pair of LiDAR latent representations as input.
elements.id-string-412: Let ($r_{s_i}$, $r_{s_j}$, $r_{d_k}$) be the latent representation for the triplet (${s_i}$, ${s_j}$, ${d_k}$) where $s_i$, $s_j \in \textbf{St}$ and $d_k \in \textbf{Dy}$.
elements.id-string-413: We construct 2 pairs from the triplet: ($r_{s_j}$, $r_{s_i}$) which is labelled as real, and ($r_{d_k}$, $r_{s_i}$), which is labelled as fake by the \textit{D}.
elements.id-string-414: In order to classify the above pairs as real and fake respectively, \textit{D} is forced to  amplify discriminatory features in dynamic scan, $d_k$.
elements.id-string-415: Instead of competing static representations against dynamic (as in a vanilla discriminator), the discrimination occurs between similarities in static scans in the  pair ($r_{s_j}$, $r_{s_i}$) v/s differences between static and dynamic scan in the pair ($r_{d_k}$, $r_{s_i}$).

elements.id-string-683: On the contrary, \dslruda{} not only removes dynamic objects and occlusion but also introduces multiple new static structures that replace the dynamic objects and corresponding occlusions.

elements.id-string-708: In this work, we address the challenge that Autonomous Vehicles(AVs) face in the absence of labelled segmentation information.
elements.id-string-709: We try to close the gap between settings that have several labelled datasets available and several label-devoid settings.
elements.id-string-710: Non-stationary object segmentation and accurate static structures reconstruction are major research challenges in these settings.
elements.id-string-711: We present a novel GAN-based adversarial model, \dslr{} that is augmented with a robust pair discriminator.
elements.id-string-712: We utilize a smartly selected LiDAR triplet using hard-negative mining that serves two purposes - generate latent pairs for the discriminator training (and) augment the discriminator with contrastive loss to increase its discriminative capacity.
elements.id-string-713: Ablation studies show the benefit of this setting over a vanilla discriminator setting.
elements.id-string-714: \dslr{} segments out accurate \textit{movable} and moving objects using static reconstructions without using labelled information.
elements.id-string-715: The generated static structures that replace dynamic objects and corresponding occlusions supplement the available static structures which improves downstream task performance.
elements.id-string-716: Our work is of practical benefit for several industrial settings - that may not have labelled segmentation and object information due to several constraints.
elements.id-string-717: We also demonstrate that our method is adaptable to datasets that lack static-dynamic correspondence information and performs well in the absence of segmentation-labels.
elements.id-string-718: \dslr{} currently is not able to surpass the performance in the labelled settings - where labelleld segmentation information is available for navigation.
elements.id-string-719: We do perform better for long sequences in the presence of high dynamism and multiple loop closures.
elements.id-string-720: These are realistic and frequent scenarios that AVs come across.
elements.id-string-721: For moderate to low dynamism sequences, segmentation based methods perform better.
elements.id-string-722: A promising future work in this direction is to find more accurate static reconstruction methods to address this gap and perform better than baselines that use segmentation information.
elements.id-string-723: Another future work of immediate interest that we have planned to work on is to develop methods that can generate  paired correspondence information from dataset that do not have such correspondence pairs available (e.g. KITTI).
elements.id-string-724: This would enable us to eliminate the need for Domain Adaptation and boost static performance for existing unpaired datasets.
